title: Exercise 3.1 — One workflow, two models
text:
In R, you can fit a linear regression directly with lm(). In this practical you will use lm() as the engine inside the familiar tidymodels steps: specify a model, fit it on training patients, and call predict() for held-out patients. In Python the same three steps are LinearRegression(), .fit() and .predict() from scikit-learn.

Part 1. Predict blood glucose from age. Calculate the prediction for a 45-year-old by hand from the fitted equation, check it with predict(), and see the point on the fitted line. Compare predictions with the measured glucose of the test patients, then refit with different training patients to see how the line and the predictions change.
Part 2. Add BMI, repeat the hand calculation, and find the prediction on the fitted plane in a 3D plot you can turn.
Part 3. Keep the same steps, training patients and predictors, and fit a decision tree instead. Follow the same patient through the splits, read the prediction from the leaf, check it with predict(), and compare the tree’s stepped surface with the regression plane.







NoteThe plots are for looking at



The code for the plots is folded away under Code for this plot (optional). You do not need to write it, but it is in the download if you want it.



RPython


Download this exercise as an R Markdown notebook (.Rmd): the text and every code cell of the R version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in Positron or RStudio and run it a chunk at a time.

Packages and data

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "tidymodels", "rpart.plot", "plotly"))

library(tidyverse)
library(tidymodels)
library(rpart.plot)

theme_set(theme_bw())

data/glucose_bmi_study.csv holds 77 patients with three columns: age in years, BMI in kg/m² and blood glucose in mg/dL. If you do not have it yet, download glucose_bmi_study.csv into your data folder.

glu <- read_csv("data/glucose_bmi_study.csv")

summary(glu)

#>       age             BMI           glucose     
#>  Min.   :21.00   Min.   :19.60   Min.   : 72.0  
#>  1st Qu.:23.00   1st Qu.:27.80   1st Qu.: 99.0  
#>  Median :28.00   Median :32.40   Median :113.0  
#>  Mean   :33.65   Mean   :32.76   Mean   :118.8  
#>  3rd Qu.:42.00   3rd Qu.:37.60   3rd Qu.:129.0  
#>  Max.   :81.00   Max.   :57.30   Max.   :194.0


Split the 77 patients into training and test patients, as on Day 1.

set.seed(14)
split <- initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8)

train <- training(split)
test <- testing(split)

cat(nrow(train), "training patients,", nrow(test), "test patients\n")

#> 61 training patients, 16 test patients




Part 1 — Predict glucose from age
The same three steps as on Day 1: specify the model, fit it on the training patients, predict.

# 1. Specify: linear regression, computed by lm()
lm_model <- linear_reg() |>
  set_engine("lm")

# 2. Fit on the training patients
line_fit <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = train)

# the learned parameters: intercept first, then the slope
b <- line_fit$fit$coefficients
b

#> (Intercept)         age 
#>  106.412332    0.348991


The fitted equation is
\[\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \times \text{age}\]

Task 1a — A 45-year-old, by hand
Read the two parameters printed above, round them to two decimals, and calculate the predicted glucose for a 45-year-old.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predicted_45 <- ______ + ______ * 45
predicted_45







TipStuck?





The first number is the intercept, \(\hat\beta_0\). The second is the slope, \(\hat\beta_1\), which multiplies the age.



Now check it with predict(), which uses the unrounded parameters:

# predict() wants a data frame: one row, one column per predictor
predict(line_fit, new_data = data.frame(age = 45))$.pred

#> [1] 122.1169


The two agree to within a few hundredths: the difference is only the rounding.


Code for this plot (optional)
ggplot(train, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_abline(intercept = b[1], slope = b[2],
              colour = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  annotate("point", x = 45, y = predict(line_fit, new_data = data.frame(age = 45))$.pred,
           colour = "red", size = 4) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "Training patients, the fitted line, and the 45-year-old")











Task 1b — Predictions against measured glucose
The test patients were not used to fit the line. Predict their glucose and put it next to what was measured.

test_results <- test |>

How far are the predictions from the measured glucose, typically?
All 16 predictions lie in a narrow band. Why?





Task 1c — Different training patients
Split again with a different seed, refit, and compare.

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
set.seed(1)
split_1 <- initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8)
train_1 <- training(split_1)

line_fit_1 <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age, data = ______)

line_fit_1$fit$coefficients
predict(line_fit_1, new_data = data.frame(age = ______))$.pred







TipStuck?





Nothing about the model changes: lm_model is the same specification. Only the training patients change, and the patient you predict for is the same 45-year-old.



Twenty different splits, twenty different lines:


Code for this plot (optional)
lines_20 <- data.frame()
for (s in 1:20) {
  set.seed(s)
  train_s <- training(initial_split(glu, prop = 0.8))
  fit_s <- lm_model |> fit(glucose ~ age, data = train_s)
  lines_20 <- bind_rows(lines_20, data.frame(
    seed = s,
    intercept = fit_s$fit$coefficients[1],
    slope = fit_s$fit$coefficients[2]))
}

ggplot(glu, aes(x = age, y = glucose)) +
  geom_point(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_abline(data = lines_20, aes(intercept = intercept, slope = slope),
              colour = "steelblue", alpha = 0.5) +
  labs(x = "Age (years)", y = "Glucose (mg/dL)",
       title = "The fitted line from 20 different training splits")















ImportantThink about it



Where do the 20 lines agree most, and where do they spread out? What does that mean for a prediction at age 25 compared with age 75?





Part 2 — Add BMI
The same specification, lm_model, with a second predictor:

plane_fit <- lm_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age + BMI, data = train)

plane_fit$fit$coefficients

#> (Intercept)         age         BMI 
#>  79.0229586   0.3216810   0.8834248


\[\widehat{\text{glucose}} = \hat\beta_0 + \hat\beta_1 \times \text{age} + \hat\beta_2 \times \text{BMI}\]
With two predictors the model is no longer a line but a flat plane above the age–BMI floor.

Task 2a — The same patient, now with a BMI of 30

# Replace every ______ below, then run this cell.
predicted_patient <- ______ + ______ * 45 + ______ * 30
predicted_patient







TipStuck?





Three parameters, in the order printed: the intercept, the weight for age, the weight for BMI.



Check it with predict():

patient <- data.frame(age = 45, BMI = 30)

predict(plane_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred

#> [1] 120.0013


Turn the plot with the mouse and scroll to zoom. The red point is the patient, sitting on the plane.


Code for this plot (optional)
# This plot needs the plotly package: install.packages("plotly")
# every combination of age and BMI on a fine grid
grid <- expand_grid(age = seq(20, 82, by = 0.5),
                    BMI = seq(19, 58, by = 0.5))
ages <- unique(grid$age)
bmis <- unique(grid$BMI)

# the plane's prediction at each grid point, as a matrix:
# one row per BMI value, one column per age
plane_matrix <- matrix(predict(plane_fit, new_data = grid)$.pred,
                       nrow = length(bmis))

fig_plane <- plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_markers(data = train, x = ~age, y = ~BMI, z = ~glucose,
                      marker = list(size = 3, color = "steelblue"),
                      name = "Training patients") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = plane_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.6, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("lightgrey", "grey")),
                      name = "Plane") |>
  plotly::add_markers(x = 45, y = 30,
                      z = predict(plane_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred,
                      marker = list(size = 7, color = "red"),
                      name = "Age 45, BMI 30") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Glucose (mg/dL)")))
fig_plane












ImportantThink about it




In words, what does the BMI weight mean?
Adding BMI moved this patient’s prediction by how much? Does a second predictor guarantee better predictions?






Part 3 — The same steps, a decision tree
Only the specification changes. The training patients, the predictors and the fit() and predict() calls stay the same.

# 1. Specify: a regression tree, computed by rpart
tree_model <- decision_tree() |>
  set_engine("rpart") |>
  set_mode("regression")

# 2. Fit on the same training patients, with the same predictors
tree_fit <- tree_model |>
  fit(glucose ~ age + BMI, data = train)

rpart.plot(tree_fit$fit, type = 3, fallen.leaves = TRUE,
           box.palette = "Blues", roundint = FALSE)








Each box asks a yes/no question. Yes goes left, no goes right. The number in each leaf at the bottom is the prediction: the mean glucose of the training patients who ended up there.

Task 3a — Follow the patient
Start at the top with the patient aged 45 with a BMI of 30. At each question, go left or right. Which leaf do you reach, and what glucose does it predict?
Check it with predict():

predict(tree_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred

#> [1] 123.4706


Turn the plot. The orange surface is the tree, the grey one the plane from Part 2.


Code for this plot (optional)
# This plot needs the plotly package: install.packages("plotly")
# the tree's prediction on the same grid as the plane
tree_matrix <- matrix(predict(tree_fit, new_data = grid)$.pred,
                      nrow = length(bmis))

fig_tree <- plotly::plot_ly() |>
  plotly::add_markers(data = train, x = ~age, y = ~BMI, z = ~glucose,
                      marker = list(size = 3, color = "steelblue"),
                      name = "Training patients") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = tree_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.8, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("moccasin", "darkorange")),
                      name = "Tree") |>
  plotly::add_surface(x = ages, y = bmis, z = plane_matrix,
                      opacity = 0.5, showscale = FALSE,
                      colorscale = list(c(0, 1), c("lightgrey", "grey")),
                      name = "Plane") |>
  plotly::add_markers(x = 45, y = 30,
                      z = predict(tree_fit, new_data = patient)$.pred,
                      marker = list(size = 7, color = "red"),
                      name = "Age 45, BMI 30 (tree)") |>
  plotly::layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "Age (years)"),
                              yaxis = list(title = "BMI (kg/m²)"),
                              zaxis = list(title = "Glucose (mg/dL)")))
fig_tree












ImportantThink about it




Describe the shape of the tree’s surface. Why is it made of flat steps?
Which predictor does the tree ask about first, and for which patients does BMI make a difference? Compare with the BMI weight of the plane in Part 2.
A new patient is 90 years old, older than anyone in the training data. What do the plane and the tree predict, and why do they behave differently?









ImportantLearning points




The steps are the same whatever the model: specify, fit on the training patients, predict for new ones. Swapping linear regression for a tree changed one line.
A linear model’s prediction can be worked out by hand from its parameters; a tree’s prediction is read by following the questions to a leaf.
The fitted model depends on which patients were used for training.
A line or plane changes smoothly and keeps going beyond the data; a tree predicts in flat steps and stays within the values it saw.

ImportantLearning points




The steps are the same whatever the model: specify, fit on the training patients, predict for new ones. Swapping linear regression for a tree changed one line.

title: Exercise 3.4 — Gradient descent
text:
Why this, here
Exercise 3.3 found the lowest point of a loss surface by evaluating 15,251 candidate lines. That works for two parameters and nothing larger. Larger models — logistic regression, and anything with a neural network in it — are fitted by the method on this page instead: start somewhere, measure which way is downhill, take a step, repeat.

RPython


Download this exercise as an R Markdown notebook (.Rmd): the text and every code cell of the R version, including the code for the plots, with the blanks left for you to fill in. Open it in Positron or RStudio and run it a chunk at a time.

The update rule
\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \alpha f'(x_n)\]

\(x_n\) is the current guess.
\(f'(x_n)\) is the derivative of the function at that guess: the slope of the tangent to the curve there. When we fit a model, the function is the MSE and \(x\) is one of the coefficients, so this slope is the derivative of the MSE with respect to the coefficient.
\(\alpha\) is the learning rate: a small positive number controlling step size.

The minus sign carries the whole idea. Where the slope is positive the function rises to the right, so we subtract and move left; where it is negative we subtract a negative and move right. Either way the step is against the slope, and the steeper the slope the bigger the step.


Minimising \(f(x) = x^2\)
The derivative is \(f'(x) = 2x\), so the rule becomes \(x_{n+1} = x_n - 2\alpha
x_n\). We know the answer is \(x = 0\), which is why this is the example: you can see whether the algorithm is working.

# Packages for this exercise. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse", "patchwork"))

library(tidyverse)
library(patchwork)

f       <- function(x) x^2
f_prime <- function(x) 2 * x

curve_df <- data.frame(x = seq(-10, 10, length.out = 200)) |>
  mutate(f_x = f(x), f_prime_x = f_prime(x))

p1 <- ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_x)) + geom_line(colour = "steelblue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = expression(f(x) == x^2), y = "f(x)")
p2 <- ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_prime_x)) + geom_line(colour = "firebrick") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0) + geom_vline(xintercept = 0) +
  labs(title = expression(paste(f, "'", (x) == 2 * x)), y = "f'(x)")
p1 + p2








Start at \(x = -10\) with \(\alpha = 0.8\) and take ten steps.

alpha <- 0.8
x     <- -10
path  <- numeric(10)

for (i in 1:10) {
  x       <- x - alpha * f_prime(x)
  path[i] <- x
  cat("step", i, ": x =", signif(x, 4), " f(x) =", signif(f(x), 4), "\n")
}

The guess goes −10, 6, −3.6, 2.16, −1.296 and so on: it crosses the minimum every single step and lands closer each time. Overshooting is not failure. With \(\alpha = 0.8\) each step is 1.6 times the distance to the minimum, so the sign flips and the magnitude shrinks by 0.6.

steps_df <- data.frame(step = 1:10, x = path) |> mutate(f_x = f(x))

ggplot(curve_df, aes(x, f_x)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey60") +
  geom_point(data = steps_df, aes(x = x, y = f_x, fill = step),
             shape = 21, size = 3, colour = "black") +
  scale_fill_gradient(low = "yellow", high = "red") +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)", fill = "step")










Task 1 — Your turn, on a function whose minimum you can check
Minimise
\[f(x) = x^2 + 3x + 5\]
Differentiate it on paper first: you should get \(f'(x) = 2x + 3\), which is zero at \(x = -1.5\). Then write the loop and see whether the algorithm agrees with your algebra.

TipStuck?





The derivative of \(ax^2\) is \(2ax\), the derivative of \(bx\) is \(b\), and the derivative of a constant is zero. The second blank is the step size, which is already defined above the loop.



Forty steps get you to −1.4995. The algorithm approaches the minimum and never arrives, which is true of gradient descent in general: you stop when the improvement stops mattering, not when the gradient is zero.


The learning rate is the whole game
Run the same problem — \(f(x) = x^2\) from \(x = -10\) — at four learning rates for twenty steps each.

descend_1d <- function(alpha, x0 = -10, n = 20) {
  x <- x0
  for (i in seq_len(n)) x <- x - alpha * f_prime(x)
  x
}

rates <- c(0.01, 0.1, 0.8, 1.0, 1.05)
data.frame(alpha = rates,
           final_x = sapply(rates, descend_1d),
           final_f = sapply(rates, function(a) f(descend_1d(a))))

#>   alpha       final_x      final_f
#> 1  0.01 -6.676080e+00 4.457004e+01
#> 2  0.10 -1.152922e-01 1.329228e-02
#> 3  0.80 -3.656158e-04 1.336749e-07
#> 4  1.00 -1.000000e+01 1.000000e+02
#> 5  1.05 -6.727500e+01 4.525926e+03


Read that table carefully, because every row is a different lesson.

After 20 steps
What happened

0.1

The fastest rate here is not the smallest one, and the boundary between working and diverging is sharp. For \(f(x)=x^2\) the step multiplies the distance to the minimum by \((1 - 2\alpha)\), so anything below 1 converges, 1 exactly cycles, and above 1 explodes. There is no warning and no error message: at \(\alpha = 1.05\) the loop runs happily and returns a number.






WarningA run that finished is not a run that worked



Nothing in any of those five runs raised an error. If you only look at the final number, the diverging run and the converging run are indistinguishable in form — both are a number. Always print the path, or the loss, and look at whether it is going down.




Task 2 — Find the edge yourself
Run the descent at learning rates either side of the boundary and identify, to within 0.05, the largest rate that still converges for \(f(x) = x^2\).

Then answer: the boundary you found is a property of \(f(x) = x^2\) and would be different for \(f(x) = 100x^2\). What does that imply about carrying a learning rate over from one problem to another?


Local and global minima
Everything above had one minimum. Now take
\[f(x) = x^4 + x^3 - 2x^2 \qquad f'(x) = 4x^3 + 3x^2 - 4x\]
which has two: a shallow one near \(x = 0.69\) and a deeper one near \(x = -1.44\).

h       <- function(x) x^4 + x^3 - 2 * x^2
h_prime <- function(x) 4 * x^3 + 3 * x^2 - 4 * x

descend_h <- function(x0, alpha = 0.03, n = 200) {
  x <- x0
  for (i in seq_len(n)) x <- x - alpha * h_prime(x)
  c(start = x0, end = x, f_end = h(x))
}

t(sapply(c(1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2), descend_h))

#>      start        end      f_end
#> [1,]   1.0  0.6930005 -0.3970463
#> [2,]   0.2  0.6930005 -0.3970463
#> [3,]   0.0  0.0000000  0.0000000
#> [4,]  -0.1 -1.4430005 -2.8334224
#> [5,]  -0.5 -1.4430005 -2.8334224
#> [6,]   2.0  0.6930005 -0.3970463



curve_h <- data.frame(x = seq(-2, 1.5, length.out = 300)) |> mutate(f_x = h(x))
ends    <- data.frame(start = c(1, 0.2, 0, -0.1, -0.5, 2)) |>
  mutate(end = sapply(start, function(s) descend_h(s)[["end"]]), f_end = h(end))

ggplot(curve_h, aes(x, f_x)) +
  geom_line(colour = "grey40") +
  geom_point(data = ends, aes(x = end, y = f_end), colour = "red", size = 3) +
  labs(x = "x", y = "f(x)")








Starting at 1, 0.2 or 2 lands on \(x = 0.693\), where \(f = -0.397\). Starting at −0.1 or −0.5 lands on \(x = -1.443\), where \(f = -2.833\) — seven times lower. Nothing distinguishes the two runs except where they began, and neither run can tell you it stopped in the worse of the two places.
Starting at exactly 0 is the strangest case: the derivative there is zero, so the first step moves nowhere and every step after it moves nowhere. Gradient descent stops at any stationary point, and \(x = 0\) here is a local maximum.






NoteWhy this does not ruin least squares



The MSE surface you plotted in Exercise 3.3 is a bowl with one minimum — convex, in the technical term — so for linear regression this whole worry is moot: every starting point reaches the same answer. The worry is real for almost everything else, which is why deep learning papers report random seeds, and why “we trained it twice and got different models” is a sentence you will hear.




Task 3 — Where is the watershed
Find, to within 0.05, the starting value between −0.1 and 0.2 at which the destination switches from one minimum to the other. Predict it before you compute it.

           end = round(sapply(starts, function(s) ______), 3))



Two parameters at once
A loss has as many derivatives as it has parameters. Collect them into a gradient vector and the update rule is unchanged — it just applies to every parameter simultaneously. For
\[f(x, y) = x\sin(y) + x^2 \qquad
\nabla f = \left\langle \sin(y) + 2x,\; x\cos(y) \right\rangle\]

fxy <- function(x, y) x * sin(y) + x^2
grad_x <- function(x, y) sin(y) + 2 * x
grad_y <- function(x, y) x * cos(y)

x <- 1; y <- 2; alpha <- 0.01
trace_xy <- data.frame(iter = 0, x = x, y = y, f = fxy(x, y))

for (i in 1:1000) {
  gx <- grad_x(x, y); gy <- grad_y(x, y)
  x <- x - alpha * gx
  y <- y - alpha * gy
  if (i %% 100 == 0)
    trace_xy <- rbind(trace_xy, data.frame(iter = i, x = x, y = y, f = fxy(x, y)))
}
trace_xy

It reaches \(x = -0.5\), \(y = 1.578\), \(f = -0.25\), which is the exact minimum of this function: for any \(y\) the best \(x\) is \(-\sin(y)/2\), giving \(f = -\sin^2(y)/4\), smallest when \(\sin y = 1\). Notice how much of the progress happens early — after 100 iterations \(f\) is already −0.153, and the remaining 900 buy −0.097.






NotePartial derivatives by hand, and when not to



We differentiated \(f\) twice by hand, once per variable. For a model with a million parameters nobody does that: the derivatives are generated mechanically — symbolically, as a computer algebra system would, or by automatic differentiation, which is what every deep learning framework is at bottom. Knowing that the gradient is just a list of slopes is enough to read those tools’ output.




Gradient descent on the glucose data
Now put the method on the actual problem: find the intercept and slope that minimise the MSE for glucose against age, by gradient descent instead of by lm(). The derivatives of \(\text{MSE}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \frac{1}{m}\sum (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\) with respect to the two coefficients are
\[\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \beta_0} = -\frac{2}{m}\sum r_i
\qquad
\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \beta_1} = -\frac{2}{m}\sum x_i r_i\]
with \(r_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\). The extra reading at the end of Day 3 derives them.

glu <- read_csv("data/glucose_study.csv")

descend_mse <- function(x, y, alpha, n) {
  b0 <- 0; b1 <- 0
  mse <- numeric(n)
  for (i in seq_len(n)) {
    r  <- y - (b0 + b1 * x)
    b0 <- b0 - alpha * (-2 * mean(r))
    b1 <- b1 - alpha * (-2 * mean(x * r))
    mse[i] <- mean((y - (b0 + b1 * x))^2)
  }
  list(b0 = b0, b1 = b1, mse = mse)
}

raw <- descend_mse(glu$age, glu$glucose, alpha = 1e-4, n = 1000)
c(intercept = raw$b0, slope = raw$b1, MSE = tail(raw$mse, 1))

#>   intercept       slope         MSE 
#>    3.234060    3.040203 2512.521591

coef(lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu))

#> (Intercept)         age 
#> 110.2979509   0.2886749


After a thousand iterations the descent reports an intercept of 3.23 and a slope of 3.04, with an MSE of 2513. lm() gives 110.30 and 0.289, with an MSE of 847.5.
Why is it so far off? The descent has not finished. Both coefficients start at 0. The intercept has to travel all the way to about 110, the slope only to about 0.3. But the derivative of the MSE with respect to the slope is multiplied by age (33 years on average), so at the start it is about 34 times larger than the derivative with respect to the intercept. The learning rate has to be small enough that the slope does not overshoot, and at that rate the intercept crawls: it needs about 160,000 iterations to get within 1 of 110. Make the learning rate ten times larger (\(10^{-3}\)) and the slope overshoots further at every step until the numbers blow up.
Nothing warned us. The MSE went down at every iteration and the loop finished without an error. Compare with a known answer when you have one, and always look at the loss.
The fix is to standardise both columns (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) so that both coefficients are on the same scale, descend there, and convert the answer back.


Task 4 — Make it converge
Standardise, descend with a learning rate a thousand times larger, and rescale the parameters to the original units.

zx <- (glu$age - mean(glu$age)) / sd(glu$age)
zy <- (glu$glucose - ______) / sd(glu$glucose)

slope     <- std$b1 * sd(glu$glucose) / sd(glu$age)

The update rule
\[x_{n+1} = x_n - \alpha f'(x_n)\]

\(x_n\) is the current guess.
\(f'(x_n)\) is the derivative of the function at that guess: the slope of the tangent to the curve there. When we fit a model, the function is the MSE and \(x\) is one of the coefficients, so this slope is the derivative of the MSE with respect to the coefficient.
\(\alpha\) is the learning rate: a small positive number controlling step size.

The minus sign carries the whole idea. Where the slope is positive the function rises to the right, so we subtract and move left; where it is negative we subtract a negative and move right. Either way the step is against the slope, and the steeper the slope the bigger the step.


Minimising \(f(x) = x^2\)
The derivative is \(f'(x) = 2x\), so the rule becomes \(x_{n+1} = x_n - 2\alpha
x_n\). We know the answer is \(x = 0\), which is why this is the example: you can see whether the algorithm is working.

Starting at exactly 0 is the strangest case: the derivative there is zero, so the first step moves nowhere and every step after it moves nowhere. Gradient descent stops at any stationary point, and \(x = 0\) here is a local maximum.






NoteWhy this does not ruin least squares



The MSE surface you plotted in Exercise 3.3 is a bowl with one minimum — convex, in the technical term — so for linear regression this whole worry is moot: every starting point reaches the same answer. The worry is real for almost everything else, which is why deep learning papers report random seeds, and why “we trained it twice and got different models” is a sentence you will hear.

We differentiated \(f\) twice by hand, once per variable. For a model with a million parameters nobody does that: the derivatives are generated mechanically — symbolically, as a computer algebra system would, or by automatic differentiation, which is what every deep learning framework is at bottom. Gradient descent on the glucose data
Now put the method on the actual problem: find the intercept and slope that minimise the MSE for glucose against age, by gradient descent instead of by LinearRegression. The derivatives of \(\text{MSE}(\beta_0, \beta_1) = \frac{1}{m}\sum (y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i)^2\) with respect to the two coefficients are
\[\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \beta_0} = -\frac{2}{m}\sum r_i
\qquad
\frac{\partial \text{MSE}}{\partial \beta_1} = -\frac{2}{m}\sum x_i r_i\]
with \(r_i = y_i - \beta_0 - \beta_1 x_i\). The extra reading at the end of Day 3 derives them.

import pandas as pd
glu = pd.read_csv("data/glucose_study.csv")

def descend_mse(x, y, alpha, n):
    x, y = np.asarray(x, float), np.asarray(y, float)
    b0 = b1 = 0.0
    mse = np.empty(n)
    for i in range(n):
        r = y - (b0 + b1 * x)
        b0 = b0 - alpha * (-2 * r.mean())
        b1 = b1 - alpha * (-2 * (x * r).mean())
        mse[i] = np.mean((y - (b0 + b1 * x))**2)
    return {"b0": b0, "b1": b1, "mse": mse}

raw = descend_mse(glu["age"], glu["glucose"], alpha=1e-4, n=1000)
raw["b0"], raw["b1"], raw["mse"][-1]

#> (np.float64(3.2340597363518033), np.float64(3.040202790594225), np.float64(2512.5215912023486))


After a thousand iterations the descent reports an intercept of 3.23 and a slope of 3.04, with an MSE of 2513. LinearRegression gives 110.30 and 0.289, with an MSE of 847.5.
Why is it so far off? The descent has not finished. Both coefficients start at 0. The intercept has to travel all the way to about 110, the slope only to about 0.3. But the derivative of the MSE with respect to the slope is multiplied by age (33 years on average), so at the start it is about 34 times larger than the derivative with respect to the intercept. The learning rate has to be small enough that the slope does not overshoot, and at that rate the intercept crawls: it needs about 160,000 iterations to get within 1 of 110. Make the learning rate ten times larger (\(10^{-3}\)) and the slope overshoots further at every step until the numbers blow up.
Nothing warned us. The MSE went down at every iteration and the loop finished without an error. Compare with a known answer when you have one, and always look at the loss.
The fix is to standardise both columns (subtract the mean, divide by the standard deviation) so that both coefficients are on the same scale, descend there, and convert the answer back.

title: Extra reading — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
text:
Setting up the minimisation problem
We want the intercept and slope that minimise the sum of squared residuals:
\[\min_{\hat{\beta_0}, \hat{\beta_1}} \; W, \qquad\text{where}\qquad
W = \sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i)^2 \tag{5.1}\]
Minimising the sum and minimising the mean are the same problem: dividing by \(N\) scales the whole surface without moving its lowest point. We use the sum here because it keeps the algebra clean.
A minimum of a smooth function is where all its partial derivatives vanish. There are two parameters, so there are two equations.
\[\frac{\partial W}{\partial \hat{\beta_0}} =
\sum_{i=1}^{N} -2(y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0 \tag{5.2}\]
\[\frac{\partial W}{\partial \hat{\beta_1}} =
\sum_{i=1}^{N} -2 x_i (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0 \tag{5.3}\]
Both follow from the chain rule: the inside of the bracket differentiates to \(-1\) with respect to \(\hat\beta_0\) and to \(-x_i\) with respect to \(\hat\beta_1\). These two are the normal equations, and everything below is rearrangement.






NoteWhere the gradients of Exercise 3.4 came from



Equation 5.2 and Equation 5.3, divided by \(N\), are exactly the two gradients the descent loop used. The difference between the two exercises is not the mathematics; it is that here we set the derivatives to zero and solve, while there we evaluated them at the current guess and took a step.
crumbs: 5  Extra reading — Ordinary least squares, in closed form

title: Extra reading — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
text:
Solving for \(\hat{\beta_0}\)
Divide Equation 5.2 by \(-2\) — which is allowed because the right-hand side is zero, and is the reason some textbooks write the loss with a \(\tfrac{1}{2}\) in front:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (y_i - \hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1} x_i) = 0\]
Distribute the summation over the three terms. The middle one is a constant summed \(N\) times:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i - N\hat{\beta_0} - \hat{\beta_1}\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i = 0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
N \hat{\beta_0} = \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i - \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i\]
Divide by \(N\) and use \(\frac{1}{N}\sum y_i = \bar{y}\) and \(\frac{1}{N}\sum x_i = \bar{x}\):
\[\boxed{\;\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\;}\]
Read that before going on: whatever the slope turns out to be, the fitted line passes through the point \((\bar{x}, \bar{y})\). The mean of the predictors and the mean of the outcome are always on the line.
crumbs: 5  Extra reading — Ordinary least squares, in closed form

title: Extra reading — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
text:
Solving for \(\hat{\beta_1}\)
Divide Equation 5.3 by \(-2\) as well, and expand:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( x_i y_i - \hat{\beta_0} x_i - \hat{\beta_1} x_i^2 \right) = 0\]
Substitute \(\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\) from above:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N}(\bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1}\bar{x})x_i
- \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 = 0\]
Distribute the sums, pulling the constants \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\) out in front:
\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y}\sum_{i=1}^{N}x_i
+ \hat{\beta_1}\bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i - \hat{\beta_1} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 = 0\]
Now collect the two terms in \(\hat{\beta_1}\) on one side and use \(\sum x_i = N\bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = N\bar{y}\):
\[\hat{\beta_1}\left(\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i^2 - N\bar{x}^2\right)
= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N\bar{x}\bar{y}\]
which, using the identity in the callout below for both sides, is
\[\hat{\beta_1} = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})}
{\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})^2}
= \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}\]






NoteThe identity, in six steps





\[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y}) = \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 1 — expand the product. \[\sum_{i=1}^{N} (x_i - \bar{x})(y_i - \bar{y})
= \sum_{i=1}^{N} \left( x_i y_i - x_i \bar{y} - \bar{x} y_i + \bar{x} \bar{y} \right)\]
Step 2 — separate the summation. \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \bar{y}
  - \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} y_i + \sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 3 — factor the constants out. \(\bar{x}\) and \(\bar{y}\) do not depend on \(i\), so \[\sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i \bar{y} = \bar{y} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i, \qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} y_i = \bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i, \qquad
\sum_{i=1}^{N} \bar{x} \bar{y} = N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 4 — substitute back. \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y} \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i
  - \bar{x} \sum_{i=1}^{N} y_i + N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 5 — use \(\sum x_i = N \bar{x}\) and \(\sum y_i = N \bar{y}\). \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - \bar{y} (N \bar{x}) - \bar{x} (N \bar{y})
  + N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Step 6 — combine. The second and third terms are each \(-N\bar{x}\bar{y}\), and one of them cancels the fourth: \[= \sum_{i=1}^{N} x_i y_i - N \bar{x} \bar{y}\]
Setting \(y = x\) gives the companion identity \(\sum (x_i - \bar{x})^2 = \sum x_i^2 - N\bar{x}^2\), which is the denominator.



So the complete solution, for one predictor, is two lines of arithmetic:
\[\hat{\beta_1} = \frac{\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)}{\operatorname{Var}(x)}
\qquad\qquad
\hat{\beta_0} = \bar{y} - \hat{\beta_1} \bar{x}\]
No iteration, no learning rate, no starting guess. The derivation follows the one in Berkeley’s EEP118 handout; with more than one predictor the same argument is done in matrix form and gives \(\hat{\beta} = (X^\top X)^{-1} X^\top y\), which is what lm() actually evaluates.

section: The closed form against the software
text:
The closed form against the software
Both estimators from means, a covariance and a variance, next to the fitted model:

RPython



# Packages for this page. If one is missing, remove the # and run this line once:
# install.packages(c("tidyverse"))

library(tidyverse)

glu <- read_csv("data/glucose_study.csv")
x    <- glu$age
y    <- glu$glucose

b1hat <- cov(x, y) / var(x)
b0hat <- mean(y) - b1hat * mean(x)

fit <- lm(glucose ~ age, data = glu)
rbind(closed_form = c(b0hat, b1hat), lm = coef(fit))

#>             (Intercept)       age
#> closed_form     110.298 0.2886749
#> lm              110.298 0.2886749





# Packages for this page. If one is missing, install it once from a terminal
# (in a Jupyter notebook, type %pip instead of pip):
# pip install pandas scikit-learn

import pandas as pd
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

glu = pd.read_csv("data/glucose_study.csv")
x, y = glu["age"], glu["glucose"]

b1hat = x.cov(y) / x.var()
b0hat = y.mean() - b1hat * x.mean()

fit = LinearRegression().fit(glu[["age"]], y)
print({"closed_form": (b0hat, b1hat), "sklearn": (fit.intercept_, fit.coef_[0])})

#> {'closed_form': (np.float64(110.2979509174209), np.float64(0.28867490665401285)), 'sklearn': (np.float64(110.2979509174209), np.float64(0.28867490665401274))}





Both give 110.298 and 0.2886749. Not approximately: to every digit either language will print. lm() is not doing anything more than these two lines, and neither is LinearRegression.






NoteThe covariance ratio also explains Exercise 3.4



Standardising both columns makes \(\operatorname{Var}(x) = 1\) and turns \(\operatorname{Cov}(x,y)\) into the correlation, so on standardised data \(\hat\beta_1 = \operatorname{Cor}(x,y)\) — the 0.1347 the descent converged to.

section: The two conditions the derivation imposes
text:
The two conditions the derivation imposes
Equation 5.2 and Equation 5.3 say that at the optimum, \(\sum r_i = 0\) and \(\sum x_i r_i = 0\). Those are not assumptions about the world; they are consequences of having minimised. Here they are for the fitted line, and for the hand-drawn line \(120 + 0.5 \times \text{age}\) from Exercise 3.2:

RPython



r_fitted <- resid(fit)                 # residuals of the fitted line
r_guess  <- y - (120 + 0.5 * x)        # residuals of the hand-drawn line

rbind(fitted = c(sum_r = sum(r_fitted), sum_xr = sum(x * r_fitted)),
      guess  = c(sum_r = sum(r_guess),  sum_xr = sum(x * r_guess)))

#>                sum_r        sum_xr
#> fitted -3.499423e-13 -8.526513e-12
#> guess  -1.338500e+03 -4.770050e+04





r_fitted = y - fit.predict(glu[["age"]])   # residuals of the fitted line
r_guess  = y - (120 + 0.5 * x)             # residuals of the hand-drawn line

print({"fitted": (r_fitted.sum(), (x * r_fitted).sum()),
       "guess":  (r_guess.sum(),  (x * r_guess).sum())})

#> {'fitted': (np.float64(-3.268496584496461e-13), np.float64(-1.0913936421275139e-11)), 'guess': (np.float64(-1338.5), np.float64(-47700.5))}





The fitted residuals sum to something of the order of \(10^{-13}\) and their product with age to the order of \(10^{-11}\): zero, to the precision floating-point arithmetic allows. The hand-drawn line’s residuals sum to −1338.5 and its cross-product to −47700.5.
That is a diagnostic worth keeping. If someone hands you fitted values from a least-squares model and the residuals do not sum to zero, either there is no intercept in the model or those are not least-squares fitted values.

title: Extra reading — Ordinary least squares, in closed form
section: The slope depends on the range of the predictor
text:
The slope depends on the range of the predictor
The derivation divides by \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\). It therefore returns an answer for any dataset in which the predictor is not perfectly constant, and says nothing about how large that variance is. Here is the same model fitted on narrower and narrower age bands:

RPython



bands <- list(c(21, 25), c(21, 30), c(21, 40), c(21, 81))

do.call(rbind, lapply(bands, function(b) {
  s <- glu |> filter(age >= b[1], age <= b[2])
  data.frame(band = paste(b[1], "to", b[2]), n = nrow(s),
             var_age = var(s$age),
             slope = cov(s$age, s$glucose) / var(s$age))
}))

#>       band  n    var_age     slope
#> 1 21 to 25 32   1.910282 0.6812665
#> 2 21 to 30 48   8.074025 4.1727148
#> 3 21 to 40 59  21.303916 2.2139585
#> 4 21 to 81 80 190.398576 0.2886749





rows = []
for lo, hi in [(21, 25), (21, 30), (21, 40), (21, 81)]:
    s = glu[(glu["age"] >= lo) & (glu["age"] <= hi)]
    rows.append({"band": f"{lo} to {hi}", "n": len(s),
                 "var_age": s["age"].var(),
                 "slope": s["age"].cov(s["glucose"]) / s["age"].var()})
pd.DataFrame(rows)

#>        band   n     var_age     slope
#> 0  21 to 25  32    1.910282  0.681266
#> 1  21 to 30  48    8.074025  4.172715
#> 2  21 to 40  59   21.303916  2.213958
#> 3  21 to 81  80  190.398576  0.288675





Over the full range the slope is 0.289 mg/dL per year. Among patients aged 21 to 40 it is 2.21, and among those aged 21 to 30 it is 4.17: fourteen times the full-range estimate, from a subset of the same 80 patients. Restricting the age range cuts \(\operatorname{Var}(x)\) from 190 to 8, and the covariance on top is estimated from fewer, closer points, so it is mostly noise. A slope is a property of a relationship and of the range of predictor values the sample happened to cover: when you compare your coefficient with someone else’s, compare the predictor ranges first.

Two things to think about

The derivation never mentions the data being normally distributed, independent, or anything else. What exactly does it assume?
Given that the closed form exists and takes microseconds, why is the whole of modern machine learning fitted by gradient descent?
